name: Paumarí
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source.
catalog_quote: (1) Secondary stress is placed on every odd-numbered mora from right-to-left. (2) Primary stress is placed on the antepenultimate mora; in words of less than three moras in length it is placed on the final (rightmost) mora.
sweep_summary: Only one works with stress in the title (Everett 2003, already listed); it is squarely about Paumari word stress and was downloaded open from the journal of record (Linguistic Discovery, DOI resolves 200 to journals.dartmouth.edu; PDF document/512 saved) and read: p. 23 states primary stress on the antepenultimate mora with alternating right-to-left secondary stress, final stress in sub-trimoraic words -- verbatim identical to the catalog's deciding quotation, so the fixed-strict antepenultimate coding is confirmed, not superseded. Cross-checked against the held SIL Chapman & Odmark 1964/2009 phonemic statement (p. 7: antepenult; no final stress; disyllables initial), which agrees for 3+ syllables and differs only on disyllables (a point the rule string is neutral on) and flags reduplicant-stress variation (also Everett sec. 3.6 / Chapman & Derbyshire 1991:349). No new open source surfaced: archive.org has no Handbook of Amazonian Languages vol. 3 or Rosetta 'pad' items, HathiTrust ISBN lookups are empty, De Gruyter's HAL 3 page (DOI 10.1515/9783110854374) is a bot-challenge/paywall; 348-349).

This is the same passage the catalog already quotes; this search of works with stress in the title re-downloaded it from the journal of record (previously held only as the author-site copy) and confirms the fixed-strict antepenultimate coding. VI.C p. 7: 'Stress normally occurs on the ante-penult syllable or on the initial syllable of two syllable words. Stress occurring elsewhere is marked with '.' and p. 7 'Stress does not occur on the final syllable on the word level.' (saved) -- agrees on the antepenult for 3+ syllable words; differs only on disyllables (Chapman initial vs Everett final), which the catalog rule string does not encode.

sources.note: Dedicated 23-page first-hand stress study (fieldwork with Paumari speakers; Chapman consulted). Primary stress on the antepenultimate mora (=antepenultimate syllable, CVV syllables counted as monomoraic), secondary stress on every odd-numbered mora counting right-to-left; disyllables and CVV monosyllables are stressed on the final mora (bimoraic minimal word). Analysed as quantity-insensitive right-to-left iambs with antepenultimate primary stress ('the only iambic stress system reported on with antepenultimate stress', p. 39). tone.quote: As the spectrograms show fairly clearly, the primary acoustic correlates of stress placement in Paumari are length and intensity. The pitch plots are also relevant, although they are slightly skewed at the end of each word due to the fact that these particular examples come from a list of words pronounced in isolation and so they receive phrase-final rising intonation typical of lists in Paumari. Nevertheless, in the Figures for polymoraic words, 4,5, 8, and 9, it is clear that a slightly higher pitch accompanies primary stress, even when the stressed syllable is the antepenult, abstracting from the strongly rising intonation at the end of the word.

tone.quote: No presente trabalho pretendemos tra~ar os detalhes básicos dos sistemas de constru~áo de pés e sílabas e determina~áo da minimalidade moraica das línguas da fanu1ia Arawá (Paumari, Suruwahá, Deni, Kulina (também conhecido como Madihá/Madijá), Banawá, Yamamadi, e Yara·wara). [...] Ao contrário da análise de CD, portanto, em nosso trabalho pessoal com o falante nativo Carlito Paumari, constatamos que a acentua~áo é semelhante ao sistema do Banawá (ver Buller, Buller e Everett 1993), isto é, é um sistema trocaico.
tone.locator: p. 297 sec. 1.1 'Propósito' and p. 307 sec. 3.2.3 'Acentuação em Paumari'
tone.translation: In the present work we intend to lay out the basic details of the systems of foot and syllable construction and of the determination of moraic minimality in the languages of the Arawá family (Paumari, Suruwahá, Deni, Kulina (also known as Madihá/Madijá), Banawá, Jamamadi and Jarawara). [...] Contrary to CD's [Chapman & Derbyshire's] analysis, therefore, in our own work with the native speaker Carlito Paumari we found that the stress system is similar to that of Banawá (see Buller, Buller & Everett 1993), that is, it is a trochaic system.
